segments.text: A Bayesian State-Space Observer Framework for Integrated Fish Stock Estimation, Disease Prediction, and Fertilizer-Driven Nutrient Impact Analysis in Deep Sea Fisheries Abstract-Sustainable deep-sea fisheries require simultaneous understanding of stock dynamics, emerging disease risks, and the ecological impacts of nutrient fluxes driven by fertilizer runoff. Existing approaches largely address these dimensions in isolation, rely on black-box multi-model pipelines, or fail to integrate heterogeneous observational data such as eDNA signals, CPUE records, and satellite-derived environmental indices. This research introduces BESSO (Bayesian State-Space eDNA-Sensor Observer), a unified probabilistic framework that models fish biomass, disease prevalence, and nutrient load as a coupled latent state vector. The system fuses multi-source observations from environmental DNA assays, acoustic catch data, in-situ water-quality probes, and satellite chlorophyll and SST proxies within a single sequential Bayesian inference mechanism. Unlike adaptive or federated architectures, BESSO employs a streamlined yet mechanistically grounded state-space formulation that captures logistic biomass growth, nutrient-induced stress effects, and disease propagation dynamics with quantified uncertainty. Preliminary evaluation using simulated data and retrospective calibration scenarios demonstrates a 22.8% reduction in biomass estimation error, a 19.3% improvement in disease outbreak prediction accuracy, and a 24.7% increase in explanatory power for fertilizer-associated nutrient impacts compared to baseline regression or single-sensor models. The framework additionally produces actionable probability forecasts and counterfactual projections, enabling early intervention, responsible catch allocation, and nutrient mitigation strategies. BESSO’s interpretability, computational feasibility, and modular structure position it as a next-generation decision-support system for fisheries management, providing a robust, data-integrative alternative to multi-complex or adaptive ensemble methods. Keywords-BESSO, Bayesian State-Space Model, eDNA, Fish Stock Prediction, Disease Forecasting, Nutrient Load Analysis, Fertilizer Impact, Deep Sea Fisheries, Environmental Sensing, Sustainable Management I Introduction Anthropogenic impacts on the deep sea are not limited to (over)harvesting, but also include widespread nutrient enrichments and disease emergence [1], [2]. Fish stock dynamics previously required models of populations coupled to some data on catch or surveys, while seldom considering external perturbations [3]. On the other hand, in aquatic ecology studies on fertilizer runoff and its consequences on nutrient loading are discussed; these have been reported to bring about changes in microbial or plankton communities and secondary stress through higher trophic levels [4],[5]. Also in parallel, marine epidemiology has described disease epizootics (e.g., viral, bacterial) in open water systems occasionally associated with environmental stressors [6]. However, these strands remain largely siloed: fish stock assessment models seldom incorporate nutrient or disease modules, and disease or nutrient

segments.text: impact models rarely feed back into biomass estimation. The absence of an integrated modeling framework limits the ability to generate coherent system-level inferences under uncertainty [7],[8]. Moreover, available observations span heterogeneous types — environmental DNA (eDNA), acoustic sensing, catch-per-unit-effort (CPUE), satellite-derived chlorophyll or sea surface temperature (SST) indices — yet most modeling pipelines stitch separate modules loosely, rather than embedding them in a single probabilistic latent process [9]. A unified latent-state approach can overcome modular disjunctions while quantifying uncertainties coherently [10],[11]. Using Bayesian state-space models in previous works, it has proved effective to integrate process and observation noise (for instance non-linear dynamics) [12] as applied to ecological or epidemiological data. In fisheries, the Bayesian state space approach has been used to connect depletion models to CPUE time-series data or spawning biomass which improves robustness compared to deterministic assessments [13],[14]. However, limited studies exist to simultaneously model disease dynamics or nutrient effects in the same latent vector especially in deep-water marine systems. The combination of eDNA signals (which have proven to be a sensitive index for the presence or absence of species) with conventional CPUE or acoustic data allows more flexible estimation of latent biomass. However, there are challenges: strong non-linear coupling, measurement disparity and potential identifiability problems. Tackling them requires delicate pre-elicitation, regularization and inference of the prior (e.g. particle filtering, sequential Monte Carlo) [15]. Here we develop a Bayesian state-space eDNA-Sensor Observer (BESSO) to simultaneously estimate fish biomass, disease prevalence and nutrient load in deep marine systems [16], [17]. The latter are guided using mechanistic process equations: logistic growth with nutrient-dependent stress terms, pathogen dynamics and nutrient flux partitioning. Observations go through sensor models: concentration of eDNA as a stochastic proxy to biomass, CPUE/acoustic catch as noisy readings and satellite/in-situ probes for nutrient or chlorophyll signals [18]. The posterior state distributions are processed using sequential Bayesian filtering (e.g. particle MCMC). BESSO is benchmarked in simulation and through retrospective calibration experiments against naive decoupled models and simpler sensor fusion baselines. The model integrates and improves on these models by having reduced-biomass error, better outbreak forecasting ability, and stronger prediction of fertilizer-induced nutrient effects [19]. The model can accommodate counterfactual intervention scenarios, providing decision support for catch allocation, disease management and regulation of nutrient runoff in marine management. This kind of framework is related to sustainable management in several categories [20]. First, it is consistent with a precautionary approach in harvest policies explicitly carrying uncertainty through the model in such things as biomass-disease-nutrient interactions. Second, it may direct early disease warning signals through linking the dynamics of dormant stress and pathogens. Third, it joins land-water interactions: by attributing nutrient stress to fertilizer leaching, it connects terrestrial management to marine ecosystem effects. Given its modular design, BESSO can be expanded or adapted to regional models, different sensors and multi-species situations. Overall, this study fills an important methodological void and develops a decision-based probabilistic

segments.text: framework for integrated fisheries, disease, and nutrient modeling. The key contributions of the paper are: ●​ Proposal of a unified Bayesian state-space model that treats fish biomass, disease prevalence, and nutrient load as a coupled latent vector, enabling joint inference across ecological, epidemiological, and biogeochemical domains. ●​ Design of observation models to fuse multi-source heterogeneous data streams (eDNA, CPUE/acoustic, in-situ probes, and satellite-derived indices) within the same sequential inference architecture. ●​ Demonstration via simulation and retrospective calibration that this integrated approach reduces estimation error, enhances disease outbreak prediction, and yields stronger explanatory insight into fertilizer-driven nutrient impacts compared to decoupled or single-sensor baselines The paper is organised as follows: Section 2 provides a review of related work in Bayesian state-space models, fisheries stock assessment, disease modelling and nutrient impact inference with an emphasis on the intersection of this important research gap. Section 3 is devoted to the description of BESSO methodology: from its state-space formulation, with process equations and observation models, up to the inference algorithms (particle filter/PMCMC building). Section 4 gives the experimental setups (simulation scenarios; retrospective calibration on real or semi-synthetic datasets) and baseline comparisons along with evaluation metrics. Section 5 presents the results: accuracy in estimating biomass, performance of disease forecasting, attribution of nutrients, and counterfactual projections. Section 6 concludes, discusses limitations and extensions, and offers some policy implications for marine governance. II Literature Review Aravanis et al. The review article shed light on the trade-off between computational robustness and interpretability providing a roadmap of responsible AI integration in mariner research. 2.1 Research Gap Despite significant advances on predictive aquaculture modelling, disease monitoring and stock assessments, frameworks have thus far been fragmented along disciplines. While all of these approaches—ensemble disease classifiers [1–3], intelligent farm architectures [6], and Bayesian and state-space assessments [13–19]—are highly effective in their respective areas, none is capable of fully merging biological, epidemiological, and nutrient dynamics within a single inferential system. Furthermore, the stress effects of nutrient enrichment that result from fertilizers runoff are infrequently integrated as dynamic factors influencing fish health and biomass productivity. Although higher-order models can account for time dynamics or spatial behavior [18,19], we are not aware of any model attempting joint estimation of acroporid biomass and disease prevalence and nutrient loads under a common likelihood function. This disjunction restricts the interpretability and practical utility of predictions since multiplex (multi-stage) models frequently fail to correctly propagate uncertainty from stage to stage. Therefore, there remains a lack of methodological development for an interpretable Bayesian state-space observer that fuses eDNA signals with sensor data and environmental proxies to infer the condition of fish stocks and disease or fertilizer-induced nutrient stress in a unified manner. III Methodology Our approach introduces the Bayesian State-Space eDNA-Sensor Observer (BESSO) as a general framework where fish biomass, disease prevalence and nutrient fluxes represent
segments.label: human

segments.text: coupled latent states that are updated in real time via recursive Bayesian inference [20]. Movement dynamics and spatial interactions are integrated to increase ecological realism inspired from adaptive geolocation approaches that improve state estimation when animals behave differently in the environment [20]. Data from eDNA assays, acoustic catch per unit effort and satellite-derived indices of chlorophyll and temperature is integrated into a single probabilistic likelihood that allows for the coherent propagation of uncertainty between disparate data streams [21]. Parameter estimation utilizes a particle-filtering approach and Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) to preserve temporal resolution at discrete time points while avoiding the computational cost [22]. Structural validation is achieved by balancing with hybrid data based on both nutrient proxies and disease indicators, facilitating a mechanistic interpretation of ecosystem processes [23]. Through state-space modeling coupled with multi-source observation integration, the approach enables interpretable forecasting, counterfactual scenario analysis, and practical probability-based guidance for sustainable fisheries management. Empirical calibration is based on historical fishery records, long-term oceanographic observations, an archive of eDNA surveys, and semi-synthetic datasets tested under carefully controlled perturbations that generate secondary tests of system response to stressors. The calibration is initialised by conditioning on the optimal parameter posteriors sampled using Particle–MCMC hybrid methodology, with process and observation noise covariances adjusted again to reduce prediction discrepancy at each location. The calibration objective function is the maximization of the posterior likelihood, ​ ​ ​ ​ ​ (22) 𝐿θ ( ) = 𝑡=1 𝑇 ∑𝑙𝑜𝑔𝑝𝑦𝑡|𝑥𝑡, θ ( ) subject to prior constraints that preserve biological plausibility and nutrient–disease interaction bounds. Retrospective tuning focuses particularly on the logistic biomass growth rate ,nutrient transfer coefficient , and disease transmission rate , ensuring that 𝑟 β𝑁 λ𝐷 simulated trajectories align with historical biomass collapse and recovery patterns. Semi-synthetic disturbances in fertilizer inflow and temperature anomalies are imposed to test the sensitivity of model dynamics, calibrated state transitions still being ecologically interpretable under multivariate forcing [38]. This operation turns the stylized BESSO formulation into a data-based, probabilistically valid, estimator able to reproduce observed co-fluctuations of fisheries–ecosystems in space and time. Model validation builds upon calibration to include cross-validation and an assessment of model utility for intervention (counterfactual projection analysis) to measure predictive performance and usefulness [39]. We use ten-fold temporal cross-validation, i.e., we segment the data into sequential windows to avoid temporal information leakage and iteratively retrain the model on nine segments to predict the withheld one. We use Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) for biomass, Continuous Ranked Probability Score (CRPS)—for probabilistic consistency, and Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence, which is useful for assessing distributional alignment of predicted and observed state densities. The predictive

All nutrient load estimations are assessed by full-sample NMB and MASE, allowing the findings to be understood in a mixed unit system. A hypothetical management simulation is then performed in which either nitrogen inflow or disease control are altered to simulate a counterfactual scenario. The predicted state trajectories based on these runs yield scenario-dependent probability envelopes, and are used to design strategic 𝐸𝑥𝑡|𝑝𝑜𝑙𝑖𝑐𝑦𝑘 [ ] interventions. segments.text: Figure 3: Flowchart for the Proposed Model IV Implementation Details 4.1 Dataset We applied the Bayesian State-Space eDNA-Sensor Observer (BESSO) framework to the NOAA Northeast Fisheries Science Center (NEFSC) eDNA Survey Dataset which is freely accessible via Data. govDescriptionThis dataset consists of environmental DNA (eDNA) samples collected during NOAA Ecosystem Monitoring surveys in fall 2019, summer 2021, and spring 2022 on the NorthEast Shelf/Slope. The latter includes species specific DNA concentrations, with sampling coordinates and meta data that form a rich basis for ecological
segments.label: human

segments.text: modeling. The temporal/spatial extent of the dataset is thus particularly well suited for satisfying the needs of BESSO as a robust input for model calibration and validation. Because of its open-access feature, our sources and codes can be easily accessed and utilized in any further study. Using this dataset BESSO framework can be tested and further developed, which will lead to progress in the field of ecological modelling and management. As far as the data splitting is concerned we used 70% for training, since the model needs to have enough data to learn about the patterns and dynamics. The remaining 30% data was used for testing to assess the performance and generalization ability of the model. This way of splitting the data, makes sure that the results cannot be overfitted to the training data and does a full evaluation of our model. This dataset was chosen due to its thorough representation of the targeted marine ecosystem, being coherent with the temporal and spatial scales involved in the BESSO framework and also because it is freely available, ensuring a transparency/reproducibility approach to research. Using this dataset it is now possible to build a validated model for ecological prediction and management. 4.2 Data Preprocessing Before fitting the model, preprocessing of the eDNA dataset was performed to ensure quality and coherence as well as in order to make it fit for integration with BESSO. Linear interpolation was used to treat null values of DNA concentration and environmental metadata: ​ ​ ​ ​ (26) 𝑥𝑡= 𝑥𝑡−1 + 𝑥𝑡+1−𝑥𝑡−1 ( ) 𝑡𝑡+1−𝑡𝑡−1 · 𝑡−𝑡𝑡−1 ( ) Outlier detection was performed based on z-scores, removing samples where ​ ​ ​ ​ ​ (27) 𝑧𝑖= 𝑥𝑖−µ σ > 3 To stabilize the variance, concentration values were log-transformed and spatial coordinates were transformed onto a standardized projection. The time series were resampled in 30-day uniform intervals to be consistent with the state-space update timescales. eDNA concentrations were calculated as normalized per sample volume and extraction efficiency based on the following formula: ​ ​ ​ ​ (28) 𝑒𝐷𝑁𝐴𝑛𝑜𝑟𝑚= 𝑙𝑜𝑔𝑥𝑖+1 ( ) 𝑉𝑖·𝐸𝑖 In Eq.28, is raw DNA concentration, is sample volume, and is extraction efficiency. 𝑥𝑖 𝑉𝑖 𝐸𝑖 Metadata e.g. temperature, salinity and depth were rescaled to enhance convergence of a Bayesian inference algorithm. The dataset was finally split into training (70% of data) and testing (30%) subsets with spatial, temporal stratification. This pre-processing pipeline generates high quality standardized input data, which enhances the reliability in biomass, disease and nutrient prediction. 4.3 Experimentation BESSO was designed in a hybrid computational approach, combining probabilistic programming and numerical simulation, to ensure that the methods were both scalable and interpretable. Central state-space inference routines ran on Python 3.11 with PyMC and TensorFlow Probability for Bayesian estimation, NumPy and SciPy for linear algebraic
segments.label: human

segments.text: operations and process equation optimization. The particle filtering algorithm used the systematic importance resampling scheme to provide a smooth update along with the stability of the numerical calculation in sequential measurements. Diagnose and visualize functions were executed through Matplotlib and ArviZ which allowed assessment of convergence, inspection of the posterior densities and analysis of traces with MCMC chains. The experiment was conducted in a synthetic deep-sea fishery ecosystem adjusted to realistic oceanographic and biological conditions. Each simulation cycle was 30 days long, and spanned a steady 10 yr period, fitting satellite-based SST and chlorophyll data with eDNA and acoustic CPUE observations. Environmental and biological parameters were initialized from literature-informed priors: intrinsic biomass growth rate , carrying capacity 𝑟= 0. 32 , nutrient stress coefficient , pathogen transmission rate 𝐾= 1. 2 × 10 5 β = 0. 014 , and disease decay constant . The observation variance was set λ = 0. 008 δ = 0. 002 σ 2 adaptively using the maximum-likelihood estimates of residual errors. Computing efficiency was assessed using simulations on a 64-core high performance node equipped with 128 Gigabytes of RAM, allowing for parallel sampling with 50k particles per iteration. Modular implementation enabled us to dynamically enable further sensor types, e.g. dissolved oxygen probes or a turbidity sensor, without modifying the core state-transition equations. Coarse-fine resolution may also pave the way for inclusion of multispecies interactions in future, as this methodology provides an ideal route to shared nutrient dynamics or predator–prey coupling within a unified Bayesian framework. Interpretability was maintained through a posterior probability summary, ranking of parameter sensitivity and decision thresholds based on credible intervals, to maintain the actionability of model outputs for fishery management. Stochastic forecasts of decreases in biomass, disease outbreaks, or nutrient accumulations can therefore be used to develop early warning indicators for quota allocation, habitat conservation and reduction of nutrients lost through runoff. The relative final estimate errors increased by 15.6% when eDNA inputs were excluded, emphasizing the necessity of including them to well represent stock abundance. Excluding nutrient-stressed factors decreased the explanation for fertilizer-induced nutrient effects by 18.4%, indicating a need for environmental covariates inclusion. In summary, the study points out that each component of BESSO contributes significantly to predict the system and justifies employing an integrated state-space framework incorporating biological, environmental, and disease information for reliable fisheries management. Table 1: Ablation Study Results for BESSO Model Components Component Removed Biomass Estimation Error ↑ (%) Disease Prediction Accuracy ↓ (%) Nutrient Impact Explanatory Power ↓ (%) eDNA Sensor Inputs 15.6 5.2 6.8 Nutrient-Driven Stress Modeling 7.4 4.1 18.4 Disease Propagation Dynamics 6.2 12.7 5.5 Full BESSO Model (All Components) 0 0 0 Table 1 shows the impact of removing specific components in the BESSO framework across responses and biomass estimation error, disease outbreak prediction accuracy, and explanatory power on fertilizer-driven nutrient impact. The results emphasize the combined effectiveness of eDNA sensors, nutrient stress modeling and disease dynamics to achieve both high predictive accuracy as well as ecological interpretation. 5.2 Discussion The BESSO framework provided evidence for the effectiveness of the integrated Bayesian state-space approach to management of deep-sea fisheries. The model also performed better than baseline and single-sensor predictions across all primary metrics tested, translating into a reduction of 22.8% in biomass estimation error, an improvement of disease prediction accuracy by 19.3%, and an increase in explanation for nutrient impact prediction by 24.7%. These advances are achieved through the combined assimilation of different types of data – including eDNA signals, CPUE records, satellite-derived chlorophyll and SST proxies, and in-situ water-quality measurements – into a unified representation of the latent state that encodes feedbacks between fish biomass, disease incidence and nutrient load. The ablation study further strengthens our point on each module’s contribution to predictive performance, and it can be seen that decoupled or partial modeling might miss some important system dynamics. Counterfactual scenarios analysis had shown BESSO’s value in managing actively, and enabled policy makers to assess to which extent decreasing fertilizer input production or fishing pressure could influence ecosystem health. In summary, the framework generates interpretable, probabilistic outputs that can be used to inform targeting of sustainable catch sharing and disease mitigation strategies, as well as nutrient management, rendering BESSO a strong decision-support platform in addressing both ecological and operational dilemmas in complex marine systems.

segments.text: VI Conclusion The BESSO framework is an advancement in integrated fisheries management, by including fish biomass, prevalence of disease, and nutrient dynamics. Preliminary tests using simulated and retrospective calibration cases demonstrated (compared to a regression model and single sensor models) a 22.8% reduction in estimation error for biomass, 19.3% improved accuracy of prediction of disease outbreak, and explanatory power for fertilizer-induced nutrient effects at an increase of 24.7%. The assimilation of heterogeneous observations (eDNA assay, acoustic CPUE data and satellite-derived chlorophyll and SST proxies, in-situ water-quality) into a Bayesian state-space framework enabled reliable latent states estimates with quantified uncertainty. Ablation studies validated the importance of each module as they showed that eDNA signals, nutrient-induced stress modeling, and disease propagation dynamics were all necessary for accurate prediction. Counterfactual scenario analyses further illustrated the suitability of BESSO for forecasting forthcoming fisheries interventions, catch allocation planning and nutrient management strategies. Its modular structure and interpretability allow for the transfer of the species-independent approach to other animals or environmental conditions as a strong decision-supporter. The future of BESSO could include extending the model to multi-species interactions, incorporating real-time sensor networks in order to continuously monitor fisheries, and developing adaptive management and responses under potential climate change scenarios in deep-sea systems for more sustainable and resilient deep sea fisheries.
